segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Bob Harris has won two cars and a lot of money playing Jeopardy on television. But he insists he's not that smart. What he is, he says, is somebody who decided when he was going to be on Jeopardy to take measures.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: I told my girlfriend at the time, hi. I'm rearranging the furniture now. And I need to make my house look like the Jeopardy studio. I set up low bookcases to be sort of like where the podiums were, about the same height. And I would stand there. I had a little homemade buzzer that I made out of a ballpoint pen and some masking tape.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He got bright halogen lights. And he pumped up the air conditioning to make it feel like the inside of a TV studio. He placed a big picture of Jeopardy's host, Alex Trebek, in about the spot where the real Alex Trebek stands.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: I even tried to time my meals to when I would be eating at Jeopardy, so that my whole body clock would be exactly in harmony.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So he played along with videotapes of the TV show. And he studied for months, memorizing all kinds of stuff, the guys who ran the United Nations in order, the presidents in order, rivers, the elements, British kings, the novels of E. M. Forster-- which include, by the way, Room With a View, Where Angels Fear to Tread, Howards End.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: The way to remember a lot of stuff is to build really big, goofy images. It takes an extra couple of seconds, maybe even a minute or two of thought, but then it stays better. So it's time well invested. I made this big picture in my head of a room with a view. OK, so you've got this nice, really big, like-- a friend of mine in Ohio grew up in this big mansion, so it's actually his living room in my head. So OK, it's a room with a beautiful view.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: And Howards End was the next one on the list that I just happened to have in front of me. And so Howards End , and you've got A Room With a View . I mean, how can you not have, like, Howard-- I have a friend named Howard. And so I made a 30-foot buttocks and stuck it in the window. So you have a room with a view of Howard's end where angels fear to tread. So the angels are in this room, and there's this giant 30-foot buttocks in the window.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's why the angels fear to tread there.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: Who really wants to be there, really?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All I can say is, you do not want to know how he got Passage to India in there. Bob says that a third of the answers that he gave on television-- a third-- came from cramming information into his head with these weird pictures that he would create for himself. And one of his biggest wins came when-- thanks to brute memorization-- he knew the name of an old book called The Compleat Angler, which to this day he has never read, has only the vaguest idea what it's about. And one of his biggest losses came when he could not remember the poem, "Jabberwocky."

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: And I was particularly frustrated because this was my father's favorite poem. And he recited it to me pretty constantly. And yet, when they asked me about it under pressure, I just completely choked. And so Brillig became my nickname, for some people.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I wonder if the reason why you didn't remember it was because it wasn't part of your Jeopardy knowledge, but because it was part of your real knowledge.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: I think that's exactly right. I think there are a lot of times in the game-- most of the big mistakes I ever made were like that, where it wasn't in my Jeopardy notebooks, my study materials, the almanacs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's funny. It's sort of like it was in the wrong section of your brain.

segments.speaker: Bob Harris
segments.text: Yeah, exactly. It was in my real brain, the one I walk around with that doesn't have much in it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Talking to Bob about all this, you realize that a show like Jeopardy, a quiz show, any quiz show on the surface seems like it's about facts, retrieving facts to win prizes. But what's really going on for the players is totally different than just retrieving facts. There's a whole inner world happening, an inner world that is not on TV at all, an inner world that actually may be a lot more interesting than what's in the program that's on TV.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well today, we dive in to look at that inner world, at the secret life of quiz shows. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life , distributed by Public Radio International. I'm Ira Glass. Our program today in three rounds. Round One, Gamester of Ireland is Fine. The round is about somebody who goes on to Who Wants to Be a Millionaire , and the most amazing thing he comes up with is not any fact, not any answer, it is the sheer courage to appear at all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Round Two, Dire Enigmas for Elite Fans, where we visit with some of the best quiz masters anywhere on an all-weekend, all-day, all-night quiz bender.

segments.text: Round Three, Girls in Need of a Safer Time. By the way, if you are noticing anything special about these round names, five points for you as you play along at home. Anyway, round three is an attempt to use quiz shows-- yes, quiz shows-- to change teenage girls. Stay with us.

segments.text: It's This American Life . I'm Ira Glass. Each week in our program we choose a theme, and bring you a variety of different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's show, The Secret Life of Quiz Shows. We've arrived at act two of our show. Act Two, Dire Enigmas For Elite Fans.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Every winter, there is this event at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where some of the country's very best puzzle solvers go up against the very best puzzle writers. It's called the MIT Mystery Hunt. And what it is is a series of puzzles-- word puzzles, number puzzles, scavenger hunts, picture puzzles, puzzles which don't even have a name.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And eventually what all this leads to-- this takes all weekend or longer-- what it leads to, the final answer, it leads you to a coin hidden somewhere on the MIT campus. This is a team competition. The teams are made up of MIT students, and also elite puzzle solvers who fly in from around the country for the event.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of our producers, Lisa Pollak, joined them for last year's contest. She was following a team called Dr. Awkward. And for those of you who are playing along at home, Dr. Awkward is spelled, D-R period Awkward, A-W-K-W-A-R-D. Give yourself two points if you noticed that that is a palindrome, spelled the same forwards and backwards. Here's Lisa.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: When you hang out with a puzzle team, you hear a lot of stories like Dave Dickerson's. When Dave was just a kid, he got this book. He'll never forget the title.

segments.speaker: Dave Dickerson
segments.text: Puzzles , Puzzles , Puzzles, Puzzles, Puzzles.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: Actually, the title might have just been Puzzles, but that's what the cover said. Dave was obsessed with this book. The puzzles were harder than any he'd ever seen, but he couldn't put them down.

segments.speaker: Dave Dickerson
segments.text: And I even remember when I saw one of the clues-- not an elegant clue by modern standards-- but it said, damn, I'm trying to fix these socks. And the answer was darn. The darn socks. You know, needle and thread. And I thought, I get that. And I solved it. It was the first clue I had actually solved. And I thought, I can do this. I had never been challenged this much in my life. And I didn't realize I could do it.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: Not only could Dave do it, he found it impossible to stop doing it, which is how, almost 30 years later, he ended up here, standing in an MIT classroom with the rest of the Dr. Awkward team, warming up for the mystery hunt. And by warming up, I mean they were plugging in their laptops and setting up a snack table.

segments.text: This was an experienced team with about 45 people on the roster. And when the female bartender came over, he told her about this cool new anagram he'd heard, how if you take the phrase, a dream within a dream, and rearrange the letters, you get, what am I? A mind reader.

segments.text: No, that's incorrect. Do you want to give it a shot, Jacqueline?

segments.speaker: Jacqueline
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: No, you don't? You don't want to embarrass yourself? All right, so actually it's a bear. It's a bear market. OK, don't worry about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So is that pretty typical?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yes. There started to be a creeping sensation that the questions were way, way too hard when she came out with chicken. That's where I thought, oh, OK, we have a problem.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: Here we go. 500-point follow-up, same category. What losing presidential candidate lost the use of his hand in World War II? Three seconds. Emily.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: Teddy Roosevelt?

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: No. Anybody else want to give it a shot? Come on. Bob Dole. Bob Dole. Yeah, World War II.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: With the girls out there not able to get answers, not able to get these answers, did you ever feel a little guilty? You know what I mean? Like you're doing them a disservice, you're making them look bad.

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Oh, absolutely, every day. It was one of these things where, when they had the blank stares and they were not ringing in on their buzzers, I would sort of sit there and I just had my hand on my forehead, sort of looking down, and just feeling like, what have I done? Like I have put them in this position. It is my fault that they can not answer, that in fact, not only am I not showing that girls are smart, I have put on the air that girls are stupid.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: That's really good. And actually, Lauren, that's wrong, too. So you don't get any points. I'm sorry. All right. Jasmine, are you ready? Here's your first question.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, this is a show on a network for women--

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: --and it's aimed at girls.

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why is the host a guy?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yeah, that is a great question. We actually auditioned scores of women to be hosts of the show. There was one girl who was possibly a good fit for the show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: And she was not really pretty enough to be on TV.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Are you serious?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Mmm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She was good, but she wasn't just pretty enough?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Even on this sort of pro-woman network?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Even on the we-love-you-for-what's-on-the-inside network. Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And what did you think when you saw that go down? Did you just feel like, OK, well, whatever, it's television?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, we were TV people, and so there-- and the assumption also was that if we wanted teen girls to be interested, maybe we give them a little eye candy. And the host that we chose sort of had a passing resemblance to Matt Damon. He was like a Matt Damon type.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: And here's the question. What amendment gave women the right to vote?

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [BUZZER]

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [? Kocey. ?]

segments.speaker: Woman 2
segments.text: There you go, [? Kocey. ?] It's all you.

segments.speaker: Woman 3
segments.text: Eighth? Ninth? 14th? 15th? Eighth?

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: Three seconds.

segments.speaker: Woman 3
segments.text: Ninth? Eighth? Ninth? Say Ninth.

segments.speaker: Woman 4
segments.text: The Ninth. No, wait.

segments.speaker: Woman 3
segments.text: No, no, she didn't say it.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: She said Ninth.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: Woman 5
segments.text: I'm going to guess 14th.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: That's incorrect. Actually, it's the 19th Amendment. 19th Amendment.
None of us deserve the right to vote, because we don't know that.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: That's true, exactly. So nobody gets the final question.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: None of us deserves the right to vote. Yes, exactly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So the girls can't answer most of the questions that you designed for the show. What do you do?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: You dumb down questions. You give them things that anyone of any age, of any mental capacity could possibly answer.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: Jesus is known as the son of whom?

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [BUZZER]

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [? Fane. ?]

segments.speaker: Woman 6
segments.text: God.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: God, that's right. So you're up to 4,000 points. Abby, you've got 3,250. Which one do you want to go with?

segments.speaker: Abby
segments.text: All right, I'll take This Spells Disaster.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: This Spells Disaster. Here's the question. Without fumbling, who can spell her first name backwards?

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [BUZZER]

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: Katie.

segments.speaker: Katie
segments.text: E-I-T-A-K.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: There you go. She's on the board.

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yeah, that wasn't one of my prouder moments as a question writer.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: Which one would you like to go with?

segments.speaker: Woman 7
segments.text: I'll take Sign Me Up, please.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: Sign Me Up, all right. This is actually a physical challenge. We want to see who can get an autograph on their arm from the cutest boy in the audience.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [BUZZER]

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: All right, Rachel, here you go. Here's a pen. You've got 15 seconds. Go right now. 15 seconds. Come on, cheer for her. 15 seconds.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: [CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So in this one, they're running through the audience with pens. And isn't this pretty much exactly the kind of boy crazy culture that you were trying to not encourage?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yes. This was pretty much exactly the opposite of what we were trying to show with the show. And that did kind of made me sad that here are these-- they're the ones who are on air and who should be the role models. And it was pretty disappointing to realize that, even though we were trying to find them and to show this, we were failing at it.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: What would be your dream car?

segments.speaker: Woman 8
segments.text: Um, I guess my dream car would be a Mustang.

segments.speaker: Ian Kesler
segments.text: A Mustang. Like a new one or an old one?

segments.speaker: Woman 8
segments.text: Whatever. Like, I probably--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so, when you got into this, your whole idea was, like, OK, let's show how smart girls are. And at the end of this experience, how did you feel?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: I felt girls are dumb.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Girls are dumb.

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Girls are dumb.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Just listen to yourself.

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: I know. This experience remains one of these things that I'm not entirely sure how to explain. I do think women are smart. But the lesson of what I saw versus what I want to believe is very different.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But is it possible the girls were smart but just not smart in a way that could be made apparent in a trivia quiz?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yes. I just think that, for a lot of it, the girls seemed much more interested in just sort of showing this really superficial side to themselves, that it was all about sort of what they looked like, and it was all about how they were presenting themselves, as opposed to what was more on the inside, or what seemed like good things to achieve.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I wonder if just in the end your mistake was you just thought more people were like you than really are. And that's the mistake that runs the world, basically.

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, I think that's probably the case. Probably not many other girls were spending their weekends playing Trivial Pursuit with their friends. But I no longer feel like it is mine to try and improve the quality of girls. That was maybe an idealistic something that I had in my 20s.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because you don't think they need it or because you think it's hopeless?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Because I don't-- I'm not sure it's possible.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Robin Epstein
segments.text: Yeah. I'd like not use the word, "hopeless," but hard, certainly. And I don't know what can. I think there's just-- I mean, I think that there can be a role model, per se, that maybe could have this influence. But it's not a game show. Certainly coming up with a quick fix, or a quick answer, or ringing in for something at the buzzer doesn't seem like the long-term solution.
